items.body: A veteran of groundbreaking music-video and visual collaborations, Ben Stokes puts his most personal stamp on Dimensional Holophonic Sound (DHS), his singular project blending acid electronics, old-school analog imagery, and experimental video production. Simultaneously, Stokes has built a distinctive career at the intersection of sound, art, technology, and visuals. Inside Ben Stokes’ vinyl obsession Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Benjamin Stokes could exist solely as a collaborator with other artists and his resume would remain an envious one. He has directed music videos for giants like Nine Inch Nails, Public Enemy, Ministry, The Orb and Meat Beat Manifesto, the latter of which he’s also a band member alongside industrial dance music pioneer Jack Dangers, whom Stokes additionally collaborates with in another outfit called Man From Mantis. He has created visuals for DJ Shadow‘s live sets, directed hype video for the Dallas Cowboys, and even helped pull off the feat of M.I.A. and Janelle Monae performing as holograms at each other’s live shows, simultaneously, on opposite coasts of the United States. And this is only a small scratch on his winning lottery ticket of collaborations. Dimensional Holofonic Sound (DHS) however, is singularly Ben Stokes. “I love collaborating with people but I think every artist needs a solo project,” he says. “Something that is their own signature and unique flavor.” I spoke with Stokes—ironically as he took a break from creating visuals for DJ Shadow‘s upcoming Endtroducing 30th Anniversary tour—to talk about his new DHS album, Concept Record, AI art, love of acid music, and any upcoming plans for live shows. “[Concept Record] is kind of like a big love letter to vinyl itself,” says Stokes. “I mean, the concept is, ‘The record is the concept.’ It’s all about vinyl. It’s an art object. I went to art school and I was trained to make objects, so it was very important to me.” That love of records is so grand that he took a risk, spent the extra money on the bells and whistles—including fifteen lock-groove loop tracks—and wrote his love letter on a hand-crafted double-vinyl edition of the album engineered with Anne-Marie Suenram of Suenram Productions in San Pablo, California, the only woman-owned and operated cutting and mastering company of its kind in North America. Ben Stokes and Anne-Marie Suenram engineering the lacquer cut for the vinyl edition of Concept Record. Taken from Stokes’ Instagram page. Locking into the groove :: Cutting the vinyl with its special features was a true labor of love. “It was indeed a major learning experience that challenged me to apply everything I’d learned,” Suenram says via email, “but with Ben‘s encouragement I was able to figure out what I needed to do. Ben‘s record was, and still is, the only record I’ve done with this kind of cut,” she says. “I wanted to try to do all the kind of physical, fun things that you can do only with vinyl,” Stokes continues, “like lock-grooves, beat matching and putting things at 133.33 beats per minute, which if you look at those tracks that are at that tempo, the grooves on the physical record actually kind of line up in an interesting visual way. And um, little side note, the inner disk labels, if you set your phone to 30 frames a second [and record a video] you get some semblance of a little animation there.” Honing in specifically on the logistics of creating a record with so many lock-groove tracks, Stokes brought along a favorite record from his collection called 500 Lock-Grooves By 500 Artists as a template. “Anywhere you drop the needle, it locks. [Suenram] looked at that record under a microscope and she was like, ‘I’m not sure how they did this, and we can’t do it quite this way with my machinery,'” Stokes explains. “The workaround was to create sort of like an entry ramp onto a freeway,” he says, “so there’s a little silence before each lock groove, and then it locks. It circles in on itself. And you really can’t test it, so you don’t really know if it’s going to work until you get your test pressings and at that point, I was like, well, I’m not going back.” Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Signature Ben Stokes kind of stuff :: Lucky for him, as well as for us, it worked very well and serves as another feature of the record’s concept, which is mixing the two records with each other—or with other records—on turntables. Stokes has done DJ sets with the album already, using his 500 Lock-Grooves record alongside Concept Record, and says they worked perfectly together. “Every lock groove on any record will match up with any lock groove on any other record, if you’re playing at the same speed.” He encourages musicians and DJs to post their own mixes to Instagram. “I would love to see what people do,” he says excitedly. All of these nifty features would be mere window dressing without solid DHS music at the core. “I didn’t want it to overshadow that it’s also a new DHS record,” says Stokes. “Part of it came about because I stumbled into a really funny sample, and it’s basically like [a celebrity] interviewing himself, and he’s talking about his album, and he’s like, ‘Oh, it’s just a great album. I mean, it’s what they call a concept record.’ So, that kind of sent me in that trajectory… led me down a rabbit hole. After that initial, like, kind of inspiration, then I just threw in every sample that I have of people talking about records. It’s got some acid house tracks and some minimal electronic-y stuff. I don’t know, signature Ben Stokes kind of stuff.” A good portion of Concept Record is dedicated to the acid music style DHS is known for. From dropping the “Green Acid” and subsequently being treated in the “Hospital Tent,” to the reminder of “I Can Feel It,” blooping along with “Supersonic Holofonic,” then flashing back with “Cut To Black” and “Full Blackout,” the whole middle section plays like one big, aural, acid-trip. “Yeah, there is kind of like a little storyline there,” admits Stokes. When asked what draws him to the style, he replies, “It was seminal. I went to school in Chicago in 1986, and the whole house thing was just teetering into acid. I don’t even think the term acid in 1986 was prevalent. But I was schooled on that stuff through WBMX radio in Chicago where, literally, I mean, the entire city would be listening to the same station. You’d hear it coming out of cars. On your front stoop, you’d hear it, one car going by with the Doppler effect, and you’d hear another one on the same station come in the other direction. I mean, it was just such a magical time. I was so young and that music was just totally new and unlike anything else that I had ever heard. I already loved electronic stuff, but this was just like, wow, these endless mixes of pretty much anonymous stuff WBMX would play for 4 hours on Friday and Saturday night. So that was just a really formative time for me. Definitely a really cool time, I think, for music.”   Redefining The Concept Record :: Now 40 years removed from those halcyon college days, the imagery Stokes has created for Concept Record‘s gatefold cover is decidedly 2026. While the content of many of the pictures may evoke the 1950s and 1960s in style, the artificial intelligence used to create them, as well as the music video for the album’s title track, “Concept Record​,” is apparent. “I actually hate AI,” Stokes says. “If I had found some film about a company that made a shiny silver record and everyone was analyzing it, I’m sure I would have used that.” He underscores that working in the industry he’s in, often being called in by companies as an art director for audio/visual projects, “You gotta keep up with the new tools. I spent a year just learning how to use some of the AI tools.” For Stokes it’s a reflection of this moment in time, yet he still tried to approach it from a familiar standpoint. “In a lot of ways, these images for the cover and for that video were very much like creating stock footage from possibly old educational films or something like that. I just created them in a very different way,” he says. “But it felt kind of familiar territory for me because I was thinking of it like stock footage.” Don’t expect AI creation to be the new norm for Stokes though. “You mentioned the ‘Supersonic [Holofonic]’ video,” he says, which I indeed had. “Well, that’s all found-footage. That’s very DHS.” He continues, “I’m sure that I will use [AI] again for work things, but when it comes to DHS stuff I think I’m going old school for everything going forward. It was an interesting detour and I feel like that’s something that, as an artist, I do often,” he says. “I did that video, I did this album cover, and then I canceled all my subscriptions. I’m going back to my roots. I like going outside with my camera and shooting stuff or doing stop motion animation. And I think that people are kind of probably craving a little bit more rough-around-the-edges analog look, you know?” Stokes stresses as to the musical content, “I did put a very big disclaimer on the inside that no audio was created using AI.”   The Art of the Tease :: With Concept Record being Ben Stokes‘ ode to the vinyl record, it almost begs the question as to what he’s been spinning lately. “I’ve been really getting into 45s,” he says. “I go up to my mom’s cabin in northern Minnesota and there’s like this thrift store called Rick’s Relics in Tower, Minnesota, and they just have this phenomenal collection of records. Just boxes and boxes and piles that, you know, they’re all out of their sleeves. It’s like 25 cents for a 7-inch. And I’ve been picking up all kinds, like The Trashmen, a Minneapolis band from the 60s. They’re, like, garage surf sort of style. I love a lot of that shit.” In continuing to answer the same question, Stokes pivots to Meat Beat Manifesto. “I absolutely love everything Jack [Dangers] does. I think it’s just incredible.” He admits to a little name dropping on his album. “I had to name-call Meat Beat Manifesto by naming a song, “Meat Beat Manifesto Soundcheck.” That was us at a show, doing soundcheck for a show.” Casually in the conversation Stokes drops a bombshell: “There is going to be a Meat Beat Manifesto tour early next year.” Cue the sound of a needle scratching across a record. “We’re booked to do a couple shows in Europe, and then there’s going to be some dates here [in the U.S.]. And, um, more info to come! And at some point, Jack and I are going to do probably a [Man From] Mantis album. Sometime in the, uh, indefinite future,” he teases. Does this mean new Meat Beat material is around the corner? “Yeah, well, Jack‘s always, always got new stuff coming out,” is the response. What of a DHS live tour supporting Concept Record though? “Well, I would love to,” says Stokes. “I’m trying to figure out a stealthy version that I can fit in the trunk of my car and like, you know, do at least a small mini tour. LA, I think, is pretty conceivable. And of course, when we do shows locally here in San Francisco, I get the absolute pleasure of having Jack performing with me as DHS.” You might guess what Stokes offers next: “I’m just going to have to keep you posted on that.” Perhaps Ben Stokes just came up with his next concept: The Art of the Tease. If so, it’s coming along nicely. Concept Record is available on Bandcamp. Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound    The post Chit Chat with Ben Stokes of Dimensional Holofonic Sound first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — Funny how a riff can sound modern, but I guess that's the way it works. Music moves in waves. This album feels very grabby, fresh and now. It's intricately constructed and great-sounding, ready to put any serious home stereo to the test.Where to start? The singing, where this band excels... and that groove! The drums are as much about rhythm as they are about texture. There's plenty of satisfying, head-bang-able metal riffing, paired tightly with great bass work. I'm reminded at times of classic Smashing Pumpkins, so there must be some grunge influence in there as well.The multilayered male/female vocals is a very alluring part of the PRR sound. Their voices don't just blend; they're sculpted together, fused and purposely locked in?creating more of a Beach Boys vibe than casually tagged-on harmonies.There are some definite Pink Floyd-inspired moments here too, particularly in the 12 minute title track 'Terrifying Angels". Then again, maybe I've got it backwards, the PRR take on it could inspire Pink Floyd. Time will tell, but on first listen, I felt I was listening to a masterpiece of modern progressive rock unfold before my ears. It clears out all the cobwebs of stereotypical prog epics and treads boldly into new cinematic textures and possibilities."Terrifying Angels" is a pretty jarring topic to tackle, so it's probably not going to be the "light" entry in the PRR catalogue. And while there's plenty of complexity and detail here, there's also lots of breathing room. But don't get too comfortable in those quieter passages, there's usually some musical surprise waiting around the next corner.Often the song structure seems indecipherable, dragging you at times through room after room of emotional spaces. I love how the familiar can suddenly become strange and new. The lyrics feel important simply because of the way the vocalists are emoting themAnd a shout-out to "Below Radiance," which really shows off Bruce Soord's skills as a mixer, managing all those incredible, epic synth textures without letting the whole thing turn into sonic soup.The last track, "Hold Your Wrath," is 15 minutes long but is a different kind of beast, not an attempt at the epic in a grand way, but a more understated, meditative journey. It features delicate, beautiful, intimate guitar parts, some wonderfully creative drum work, and I love that electronic bass. It feels like another experimental track for the band, though really, the whole album feels adventurous. And despite all of this, you can still bounce to this band.Prog dog score is 4.5 out of 5 dog bones, or 4 out of 5 for the progarchives system.

items._cn_summary: Pure Reason Revolution的《Terrifying Angels》在前卫摇滚框架内展现了显著的实验倾向。多层人声设计是核心特色，男女声线经过精心雕琢，和声结构复杂且充满空间感，超越传统叠唱模式。器乐层面融合金属 riff、grunge 质感与电子合成器纹理，鼓组兼顾节奏推进与音色实验。12分钟同名曲在 Pink Floyd 式氛围铺陈与新型电影化声景之间切换，呼吸感与复杂度并存。混音师 Bruce Soord 在多层合成器音色的平衡控制上表现出色，避免了密度过高导致的混浊。终曲以吉他原声质感和电子贝斯构建冥想式旅程，与专辑前半段的张力形成对照。整体在保持前卫摇滚骨架的同时，注入了当代制作理念和跨界融合意识。

items.body: Düsseldorf and Electronic music have been inextricably linked for decades. The city has produced a distinctive musical legacy in which experimentation, electronics, minimalism, and a fascination with the future have always been central. It is a history that stretches back to the 1970s and 1980s, when electronic music, with Kraftwerk as its pioneering flagship, was not so much regarded as an exercise in nostalgia, but rather as a way of looking towards the future. It was within this tradition that Mängelexemplar emerged in 2011, simply abbreviated as MNGLXMPLR. The Düsseldorf duo, consisting of Lilli B. and Joa Carisma, found their place in the international underground with a distinctive blend of Minimal-Wave and Electro-Pop. Their name — stripped of its vowels to become the almost cryptic MNGLXMPLR — seems perfectly suited to their musical universe: sleek, unconventional, and just a little elusive. Over the years, MNGLXMPLR have established themselves as a familiar name on the scene, performing at numerous festivals and venues both in Germany and abroad. With their new album, “Neue Zukunft,” released this spring on Infacted Recordings, they continue their exploration of Minimal-Wave, delivering an opus that feels darker, harder, and more intense. I spoke with both protagonists about the album, their musical journey, and the future of MNGLXMPLR. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: MNGLXMPLR has now been active for more than ten years. Looking back, what are the first thoughts that come to mind? What have been the defining moments or biggest highlights so far, and how would you say the band has evolved over the years? M:More than ten years… that’s quite a statement. The funny thing is, there was never a ten-year plan. We founded MNGLXMPLR because we wanted to make music. One year became five, five became ten – and suddenly here we are. There have been intense phases, quiet phases, great shows, frustrating moments, and countless ideas that never made it anywhere. That’s part of it. The biggest change is probably that we’ve become much more confident in our own musical language. In the beginning, there was more searching and experimenting. Today, we have a much better sense of what feels right for MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to turn that into a formula. The moment you know exactly what the next track is going to sound like, things become boring. There have been many highlights over the years – releases, concerts, travels and encounters that happened through the music. But the biggest highlight is actually very simple: we’re still here. And we’re still curious. Q: It took several years for “Neue Zukunft” to finally see the light of day. I imagine that period brought about changes – not only in terms of your studio setup, but also in your songwriting and creative process. Could you tell us a little about how you have evolved and how that development shaped the album? M:“Neue Zukunft” took its time. A lot changed at Carismastudios during those years. The studio evolved, new equipment was added, different projects emerged, and we experimented with different ways of working. Some of those experiments eventually became part of the album. There are tracks that existed for years before they found their final form. We kept coming back to them, changing things, removing things, and sometimes simply leaving them alone for a while. Our songwriting has become more intuitive over time. We don’t sit down and say, ‘Today we’re going to write a minimal track’. A song can start with a beat, a sound, a voice, or simply a certain mood. The emotional side has also become more important. We wanted the emotion to already be present in the music, rather than being added later through production. The result has become harder and more direct in some places, but the minimalist foundation has remained. And we have no problem with a few rough edges. For us, perfect doesn’t automatically mean interesting. Q: What can you tell us about “Neue Zukunft”? What is the central idea or concept behind the album, and how do you look back on the composition, recording and production process today? M:“Neue Zukunft” is about change and movement. It’s not a concept album in the classic sense. There isn’t one single story that you have to decode. It’s more like a collection of different moods and sides of MNGLXMPLR. Minimalist structures, darker atmospheres, harder sounds and emotional moments. We wanted to preserve these contrasts. The visual identity also became an important part of the album. For this, we are working with Düsseldorf fashion icon Ela Holscher, fashion designer Michaela Reinhardt-Beron and photographer Thomas Stelzmann. In Düsseldorf, music, fashion, photography and art have always been closely connected. So for us, this connection felt very natural. But we didn’t want to turn it into nostalgia. We have no interest in pretending it’s 1982 again. Düsseldorf has its history. We’re interested in what we can do with it today. This idea is also carried onto the stage. Sound, visuals, fashion and performance should become part of the same atmosphere. Q: The title “Neue Zukunft” immediately catches the eye – particularly at a time shaped by increasing geopolitical tensions, social uncertainty and war. At the same time, we are entering a new artistic era in which algorithms, AI and digital technologies are increasingly influencing how music is created and consumed. What does the title “Neue Zukunft” mean to you, and how does it reflect your view of the world today? M:We deliberately wanted a title that looks ahead. There is already enough dystopian language around us. Of course, we see what is happening in the world. War, political conflicts and uncertainty are part of the present. But “Neue Zukunft” is not about resignation. It’s about movement. The future is coming anyway. AI is obviously part of that future and is already changing the way music is created and consumed. We don’t use AI to create MNGLXMPLR. For us, the human process remains essential: writing, playing, recording, making mistakes and changing things. Electronic music, however, has always been closely connected to technological change. Synthesizers, samplers and computers changed the way musicians work. AI will be another major shift. We don’t think it makes sense to simply accept it blindly or reject it outright. You have to question it. You have to decide what you want to use from it and why. “Neue Zukunft” doesn’t mean that we know what tomorrow will look like. It means that we’re ready to find out. Q: These days, many listeners focus more on playlists and individual singles than on complete albums. I personally still believe that an album represents a comprehensive artistic statement. Do you think the album format remains relevant in an increasingly fragmented and fast-paced musical landscape? M:Absolutely. A single can work on its own. But an album gives it context. You can build an atmosphere, create tension and connect tracks that might work very differently as individual singles. That’s important to us. “Neue Zukunft” was made as an album, and the sequence of the tracks matters. And then there’s the album on vinyl. We like the physical experience. You take the record out of the sleeve, look at the artwork, put it on and listen. Then you turn it over. You can’t really speed that up. And maybe that’s exactly the point. In a world where everything is instantly available, a record forces you to slow down. You can even hold the music in your hands. Artwork, photography, design and music become one shared object. That still has value. Q: MNGLXMPLR is also very much a live band – you have even played in Belgium three times already. How important are live performances to your identity as a band? How do you transfer the atmosphere of your studio recordings to the stage, and what touring plans do you have in connection with “Neue Zukunft”? M:Playing live is extremely important to us. The studio is controlled; the stage isn’t. That’s exactly why we like it. We don’t want to simply reproduce “Neue Zukunft” live exactly as it sounds on the record. The live versions are more direct, more physical and sometimes even harder. But the atmosphere has to remain intact. The audience also changes the performance. You can prepare a set, but you can’t prepare a room. We’ve already played in Belgium three times, and every concert had its own character. That’s one of the reasons we enjoy playing abroad. With “Neue Zukunft”, we want to play a new series of concerts across Europe. Looking towards 2027, we also want to move beyond the classic minimal scene, discover other Electronic scenes and play larger stages. The visual side will also become more important. Not as decoration, but as part of the performance. Sound, light, fashion, photography and movement should belong together. We don’t want people to simply hear “Neue Zukunft”. We want them to experience it. Q: You come from Düsseldorf, a city that will forever be associated with KRAFTWERK. To what extent do you still feel this artistic legacy among Electronic artists from the city today? Has Düsseldorf’s musical heritage directly or indirectly influenced your own work? M:Kraftwerk is unavoidable. If you make Electronic music in Düsseldorf, you grow up with that history. But Düsseldorf is much more than Kraftwerk. DAF, Die Krupps and many other artists developed completely different forms of electronic music. What connects them for us isn’t necessarily a particular sound. It’s an attitude: experimenting, reducing, making music physical, questioning things, and not caring too much whether someone has already invented a genre for it. We can relate to that a lot. But we don’t want to sound like Kraftwerk, or DAF, or Die Krupps. They’ve already done that – and pretty well. So our connection to Düsseldorf’s musical history is more indirect. You grow up surrounded by music, art, fashion, photography and clubs. You absorb that environment without necessarily realizing it. And years later, you realize how much of it has stayed with you. So yes, Düsseldorf has influenced MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to become a heritage band. We respect the past, but musically, we live in the here and now. Look back. Take with you what matters. Keep moving forward.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以采访形式呈现，聚焦杜塞尔多夫二人组MNGLXMPLR的新专辑《Neue Zukunft》。乐队延续了德国电子音乐传统，融合Minimal-Wave与Electro-Pop元素，新作相比以往更为黑暗、坚硬且富于强度。采访中两位成员回顾了十余年的创作历程，从早期对声音语言的探索到如今形成更为自信的个人表达，他们强调对持续实验的兴趣，拒绝固守80年代复古美学。专辑制作在Carisma Studios完成，期间录音设备与创作思路均有显著迭代。乐队活跃于德国及国际地下场景，签约于专注暗潮与工业电子领域的Infacted Recordings。整体呈现一种根植于杜塞尔多夫电子传统的当代暗色电子声音，既有类型延续性也体现了创作者对音乐语言边界的持续追问。

items.body: I went to bed I saw you there You shook your head It’s all out, where? There is a special cruelty in being wounded by someone who has already left the room. The accusation lands, the door closes, and suddenly one person possesses the luxury of departure while the other inherits everything that remains unresolved. They replay every sentence, defend themselves to an empty room, and search for the words they were never allowed to speak. Kind Kid’s latest single bleed inhabits precisely that imbalance, turning abandonment into a bright, brisk synthpop song whose surface seems almost indecently cheerful beside the injury underneath. The arrangement draws its movement from eighties synthpop and its darker hues from the gothic electronics of Clan of Xymox to the Modern Darkwave sensibilities of Boy Harsher, with eerie synth flourishes and cold, uneasy tones curling around a dark disco beat. The rhythm keeps the song moving toward the dance floor, though something in those keyboards suggests the argument will be waiting when you get home. Julien Martinez sings from the position of someone denied the final word, his sense of injury finding an accomplice in the music’s disquiet. That tension gives “bleed” its emotional force: the hooks offer release while the synths keep returning to the bruise. The lyrics are deliberately circular. Images return, phrases repeat, and the speaker seems trapped inside an encounter that has ended everywhere except in his own mind. Repetition becomes psychological rather than decorative, suggesting those arguments one continues hours later while washing dishes, driving home, or staring at the ceiling, inventing increasingly perfect replies for someone who is no longer listening. “I thought of it as some metaphorical situation where someone’s been left behind after some sort of attack… left to “bleed,” muses Kind Kid frontman Julien Martinez. “Sometimes a situation can feel so much different to one person than the other.” One person may regard an argument as a momentary discharge of anger; the other can experience the same exchange as an injury requiring days to understand. bleed catches that disparity without weighing down its pop architecture. Its hooks remain airy, almost playful, while the words circle rejection, exposure, and helplessness. Listen to bleed below and order the single here. bleed by kind kid Recorded at Golden Dice Studios in Brooklyn, the track was produced by Dutchrevz and Kind Kid, then mixed and mastered by Michele Ricci. bleed is Kind Kid’s final single before the album arrives October 9th. Follow Kind Kid: Instagram Threads Bandcamp The post NYC’s Kind Kid Dresses an Open Wound in Haunting Dark Synthpop Single “Bleed” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: Kind Kid的单曲《bleed》以八十年代合成器流行为骨架，融入Clan of Xymox式的哥特电子质感与Boy Harsher式的现代暗潮氛围，在明快的舞曲节奏与阴冷的键盘音色之间制造持续张力。主唱Julien Martinez从被遗弃者的视角出发，用循环往复的歌词结构模拟一个人在空房间里反复排练未说出口的辩驳，让重复成为心理创伤的外化形式而非装饰手段。制作上由Dutchrevz与乐队共同在布鲁克林Golden Dice Studios完成，节奏虽指向舞池，合成器纹理却始终暗示归家后未完的争吵。整首作品在流行架构内承载了关于伤害不对称性的思考，旋律的轻盈与情绪的淤青构成鲜明反差，是暗潮与合成器流行交叉地带中一次成熟的表达。

items.body: Are we better off alone Will I come into my own Are we better off alone Being understood by someone is a comfort until the relationship ends and their imagined opinion starts conducting an inspection of everything wrong with you. Boy Harsher’s Faulty inhabits that uncomfortable interval between asking to be wanted and wondering what that wanting has cost. Jae Matthews sings as though the verdict may already be in, while Augustus Muller gives her doubts enough room to move. The question of being better off alone becomes something to turn over on the dancefloor, where thinking clearly has always been optional. The song accompanies the release of Get Mean, out now following its September 18 arrival through Atlantic Records. Their first album since 2022’s The Runner, the twelve-track record follows the end of Matthews and Muller’s romantic relationship in early 2024, after a period of family loss, personal upheaval, and creative uncertainty. Continuing the band meant finding a way to work together while the terms of their lives were changing. That makes the tenderness of Faulty particularly affecting: the people making this music understand how complicated its questions can become. A kicking beat, busy hi-hats, and quivering synths set Faulty in motion. Its dark disco rhythm has some of Careful’s physical insistence, softened by broad synth pads and little descending electronic notes that drop through the arrangement with a rounded, almost playful boop. When the beat pauses to breathe, the synths take on a Vangelis-like warble, briefly opening the song into something more spacious and cinematic. The rhythm returns beneath a lead synth that bends up and down in pitch, while Matthews keeps her voice hushed and close, breathing the words with a tenderness that borders on resignation. The lyrics put affection and self-assessment in an uncomfortable room together. Asking whether she is faulty gives another person the power to diagnose her; asking whether she will come into her own begins to take some of that power back. Repetition keeps either possibility from becoming a settled conclusion. Matthews sounds caught between wanting to be held and recognizing how much of herself might be waiting outside the relationship. Directed by Boy Harsher and shot on 35mm with cinematography by Owen Smith-Clark, the final video in the Get Mean series returns to a room lined in brown wood paneling. A television glows blue on a black stand, a small fan sits by the window, and a microphone cable trails across the carpet. Against that ordinary setting, the changing cast look dressed for entirely different evenings: a white cowboy hat, metallic bodysuits, striped knitwear, black boots. Each person seems to have brought a private version of the same bad night. The camera moves from fixed views of the room into close-ups of faces, hands, and bodies moving past one another. People share the frame, lean together, or briefly touch, but proximity never quite settles the question in the chorus. There is a lovely awkwardness to it: the self-consciousness of dancing at home, followed by the sudden absorption of forgetting you are being watched. By the end, the people have gone and the television is still there. The room has held all that feeling without offering anyone an answer. Watch the video for Faulty below: Across Get Mean, the effort to keep going takes several musical forms. Writing began to move again when Matthews took to the road, travelling through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and South Florida. The album was eventually recorded in eight locations across the United States, Mexico, and Italy, its unsettled circumstances allowing new sounds and approaches into the duo’s work. Matthews describes it as “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” The three singles we covered ahead of its release made clear how much that offering could contain. The first indication came with Jeans, released in June. Its springy guitar figure and bubbling electronics brought a new wave directness to Boy Harsher, with a steel-slide twang giving the song a western accent. Our earlier comparison to the Pretenders still fits the way Matthews’ cool delivery rides that guitar, while the buoyancy also suggests Muller’s work in Safe Mind. Beneath the cheek is a sharp little study of ambition: the dream of escaping a small town, the dream of becoming somebody, and the possibility of ending up selling an image of freedom by the pair. The band’s latex line-dancing video, conceived with Robert Palmer’s Addicted to Love in mind, makes that collision between aspiration, performance, and merchandise deliciously literal. Hard Beat, unveiled alongside July’s album announcement, tightens the pressure around a repeating bass-synth figure and an unrelenting kick. As we noted then, there is something of Depeche Mode’s Behind the Wheel in its meeting of motion, desire, and surrendered control. Matthews moves between confession and invitation while the rhythm keeps pushing ahead. Its video makes those exchanges physical through an elaborate leg brace, a Cadillac, and a handheld camcorder, drawing medical hardware, automotive controls, and the invasive act of filming into the same uneasy visual language. Within the album, the track preserves the severe club momentum that has long served Boy Harsher so well, giving the softer and more openly melodic songs something solid to push against. August’s Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call) puts a warmer arrangement around the indignity of waiting for someone to remember you exist. A brisk new wave beat, rounded bass, bright keyboards, and short bursts of distorted guitar carry Matthews’ unhappy drawl toward the sort of pop chorus that can make despair briefly feel sociable. Her insistence that she is okay sounds increasingly like something she needs to practice. Our earlier review followed that idea into the lyric video, where yellow karaoke lettering crosses the blue screen of a CRT television. Created with vintage video equipment by Sean McGuirk and shot by Jesse Korman, it turns failed communication into a singalong with nobody else visibly present. Heard beside Faulty, the song makes the eventual question of solitude feel earned. Coming Home opens with Matthews in a smoky, Lynchian register, her voice suspended over steadily repeating synths and a breezy dance beat. The low guitar tones bring New Order to mind, with the melodic weight of a Peter Hook bassline translated onto guitar. That combination gives the song an appealing pull between bodily ease and emotional uncertainty. The rhythm leaves the windows open; the vocal suggests someone still deciding whether it is safe to come inside. Here, the album’s broader musical interests allow vulnerability to sound inviting without making it seem simple. Ice Pick (Walk Away) makes a particularly satisfying turn toward gothic rock. The parenthetical invites a Sisters of Mercy comparison before the guitar has even had its say, and the melody strengthens the association with their First and Last and Always period. A deep post-punk bass groove and the crunchy splash of the drum machine give the track a familiar dry ice chill. Matthews’ tender delivery moderates that severity, placing a vulnerable voice inside an arrangement with its collar firmly turned up. The resemblance is a pleasure to hear, especially from a duo whose love of this music has often been expressed through a different set of instruments. Pray 4 Me lets the bass loosen its hips. Soft synth pads, a sexy funk groove, and quivering bell tones bring a strain of Bryan Ferry-eque sophisti-pop into the album, expanding its capacity for pleasure as well as distress. There is a suppleness to the arrangement that makes this feel like a natural extension of the record’s emotional dynamic range. Desire, after all, does not become less complicated when somebody gives it a particularly good bassline. Boy Harsher sounds comfortable letting elegance and appetite share the same song. The album closes with Bleed, setting trip-hop beats against crystalline synths and low, bone-marrow-churning bass. Imagine the Bristol-born genre taking shape inside the electric dreams of the mid-1980s: the drums with a twitching hi-hat and thump have that low, unhurried weight, while the electronics give the space around them a cool, glassy clarity. After the movement of the preceding songs, this slower finish lets the record exhale. Its change of pace offers a place to sit with everything that has happened. Get Mean gives Matthews and Muller’s affection for post-punk, synthpop, goth, and dance music considerably more room to misbehave. They have grown as people, their lives have changed, and their music has had the good sense to evolve. Those expecting Pain on an endless loop, or Careful with a fresh set of track titles, may find this development inconvenient. For listeners who share Jae and Gus’s musical curiosity, there is pleasure in hearing them loosen up, follow their enthusiasms, and discover what this new chapter of their partnership can become. And if Get Mean isn’t the Boy Harsher you ordered, well, tough shit. Listen to Get Mean below and order the album here. Additional listening and purchase options are available here. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Since forming in 2014, Matthews and Muller have taken Boy Harsher from the small cassette run of Lesser Man, whose Pain spread widely online, through Yr Body Is Nothing in 2016, the Country Girl EP in 2017, and Careful in 2019. Their background in film became central to 2022’s The Runner, which they wrote, produced, directed, and scored. Their work in cinema also includes The Lonely Woman, their debut feature as directors, starring Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, and Sturgill Simpson. Boy Harsher’s The Heartbreak Tour resumes September 25 at Basilica Hudson, with North American dates running through November 5 at New York’s Knockdown Center. The European and UK run begins November 14 in Lyon and includes London’s Roundhouse on November 29. Choir Boy joins select dates. Visit the band’s shows page for tickets and current availability. items._cn_summary: Boy Harsher在新专辑Get Mean中将个人生活的断裂转化为舞池上的拷问。主唱与制作人身份的恋人关系结束后，两人继续以乐队形式合作，使得这张十二曲录音带有某种内省的重量。单曲Faulty以暗色迪斯科节拍构建骨架：踢鼓与密集的踩镲推动节奏，合成器铺陈宽厚声场，下行电子音符以圆润的弹跳感穿插其间。当节奏短暂留白时，合成器呈现近似范吉利斯的颤音质感，将空间短暂撑开为某种电影化的广袤。人声贴近麦克风低语，气息与咬字带着温柔与放弃之间的暧昧张力。歌词在渴望被接纳与怀疑被审视之间反复摇摆，重复句式阻止任何一端成为定论。MV以35毫米胶片拍摄，在棕色木墙房间的日常陈设中，多组人物穿着风格迥异的服装交替出现，身体接近却始终无法真正靠近，将歌词中的疑问转化为画面语言。

items.body: ケイシー・カンジェローシ 初来日リサイタルに寄せて 世界中のパーカッショニストを魅了する演奏家・作曲家、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。その初来日リサイタルが、2026年9月26日（土）、長久手市文化の家 森のホール（愛知県）で開催される。公演に寄せられた3人のコメントと映像から、その魅力を紹介する。 打楽器音楽の常識を覆す発想 新野将之（マルチパーカッショニスト） 僕が最も敬愛する打楽器奏者、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。 彼の音楽には、「打楽器でここまでできるのか！」という驚きが詰まっています。卓越したテクニックはもちろん、タンバリンやスネアドラムの可能性を極限まで追求し、石を打ち合わせる音、電子音、パントマイムまで音楽の中へ大胆に取り込んでしまう。その発想は、まさに打楽器音楽の常識を覆すものです。 そして何より面白いのは、彼の音楽が「聴く」だけでは終わらないこと。音、身体、動き、空間……すべてをひとつの表現として融合させ、クラシック音楽の枠を飛び越え、新しいエンターテイメントへと昇華させていきます。 アートでありながら、圧倒的に楽しい。 知的でありながら、魂を揺さぶる。 打楽器の未来を切り拓いてきた開拓者、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。その唯一無二の世界を、ぜひ生で体感してください！ ﻿ 身体表現と、超絶技巧の打楽器演奏を一体化 小室敬幸（音楽ライター） 1982年にアメリカで生まれたケイシー・カンジェローシは、打楽器を音だけでなく、奏者の身体や身振りまで含む舞台表現として捉えているユニークな打楽器奏者で作曲家だ。今回のリサイタルで演奏されるティエリー・ドゥ・メイ《Silence Must Be!》は、その志向を象徴する選曲である。メイはローザスを率いるアンヌ・テレサ・ドゥ・ケースマイケルら、ベルギーのコンテンポラリーダンスと密接に活動し、音楽的にはルイ・アンドリーセンらに連なるヨーロッパ的なミニマリズムを結びつけた作曲家。そのメイのような音楽の系譜に位置づけられるカンジェローシは、代表作《Meditation No.1》を含む自身の作品でも、打つ、振る、構えるといった動作や反復が、音と同じほど重要な表現になる。ダンスや演劇に通じる身体表現と、超絶技巧の打楽器演奏を一体化させており、今や世界中の若いパーカショニストを魅了している作曲家なのだ。目で見て真価が味わえる音楽なので、日本で初めて行う本格的リサイタルは必聴・必見である！ フィクションとフィジカルのあわい 加藤綾子（ヴァイオリニスト） YouTubeやInstagram上で切り抜かれる、カンジェローシの身体。バストアップであったり、手元や指先であったりするそれらを画面越しに見たとき、わたしたちは、まずそのディテールに心を奪われる。その身体は多彩な楽器を、ごく当たり前に扱う（ように見える）。ティエリー・ドゥ・メイのスコアを、美しく実現する。石ころもオルゴールも、スティックも、あまりに自然に振る舞うものだから、まるでオブジェクト・シアターを鑑賞しているような感覚に陥る。 そのうえで、彼は切実な演奏者であり続ける。鍛錬された身振りは、どこまでいっても彼自身あるいは他者の音楽を実践し、批評するためにある。その切実さが、きっと、ひとびとの全身を鷲掴む。画面越しではない、実存として長久手に立つ「カンジェローシ」は、音楽というフィクションとフィジカルのあわいを鮮やかに描き、突きつけてくれるだろう。──つまり、生で見るカンジェローシの演奏は、めっちゃすごくてやばいはず、ということです。 公演情報 ケイシー・カンジェローシ パーカッションリサイタル TENDRILS 2026年9月26日（土）16:00 長久手市文化の家 森のホール（愛知県） 公演詳細：https://bunkanoie.jp/archives/9250

items.body: Happy Sunday, here’s a quick shot of some irreverent fun for the end/beginning of your week (depending on how you set up your calendar): Kuhn Fu, the eight‑member ensemble led by guitarist‑composer Christian Kühn mixes a bit of rock energy with jazz freedom. "Free improvisation-only" folks may wrinkle their noses at such a description, but take a listen - would Frank Gratkowski , John Dikeman or Ziv Taubenfeld lead you astray? Video is from Zentrifuge, Berlin in October 2025. Christian Kühn - guitar, composition Frank Gratkowski - alto sax, flute, clarinet John Dikeman - tenor sax Mateusz Rybicki - tenor sax, clarinet Ziv Taubenfeld - bass clarinet Sofia Salvo - baritone sax Esat Ekincioglu - bass George Hadow - drums More: https://kuhnfumusic.com/ 2026 FILMED BY EAR is a series by @berta.berlin . items._cn_summary: 这是一支由吉他手兼作曲家Christian Kühn领导的八人乐队Kuhn Fu!的现场视频，来自柏林Zentrifuge，2025年10月录制。乐队成员配置颇具特色：三位管乐演奏者分属中音萨克斯/长笛/单簧管、次中音萨克斯与低音单簧管不同声部，再加上两把次中音萨克斯/单簧管与上低音萨克斯，形成厚重的复调层次。吉他、低音贝斯与鼓构成了节奏核心。乐评指出这支乐队将摇滚的能量感与爵士的自由即兴相融合，可能让纯粹的即兴乐迷感到不适，但建议实际聆听后再做判断。乐队阵容汇集了Frank Gratkowski、John Dikeman、Ziv Taubenfeld等活跃于欧洲即兴圈的乐手，保证了演出的实验性与可信度。整体呈现一种戏谑而不失严肃的折中态度，是欧洲地下自由爵士场景的一次跨界尝试。

items.body: Richard J. Birkin’s official soundtrack to Jon McGregor’s Reservoir 13 was written, performed, and recorded live with Haiku Salut, an instrumental trio from the English Midlands. The book was awarded the 2017 COSTA Novel of the Year, and its soundtrack wears the same shoes; its blue threads help in framing a photograph of sudden loneliness, its strings wrapped up in midwinter mystery. Described by The Guardian as ‘a chilling meditation on loss and time’, Reservoir 13’s soundtrack is equally cool-blooded. The strings search for missing 13-year-old Rebecca, the sudden loss of light shrivelling the music into a sluggish state of shock. The unexplained and instantaneous earthquake, an event as cataclysmic as the one in Don DeLillo’s Point Omega, sends an endless ripple through tomorrow. Everyone’s looking for answers – crime or no crime – but life doesn’t work like that; the Universe isn’t required to offer a neat resolution or a form of closure. For the most part, things drift. People drift. Unexpected, and often terrible, events happen each and every day. Threads often just run out, with no explanation given, and no end to suffering in sight. No resolving. But, for Birkin, this is potent material. Strings swell slowly, and that gives the music more of an edge. Paradoxically, an unstoppable force, screaming at the top of its lungs, can be felt inside the quiet, caressing motion of the bow. A muted scream. Whenever McGregor was at a book reading, Birkin’s technology allowed the writer access to the phones in the audience, creating a communal experience as the reciting of words, along with an unfolding section of the story, met with audience participation – and, of course, this produced a number of different outcomes. Not one reading was ever the same. The piano has always lent itself to deep pools of thought and sliding melancholia, but in this case it’s gut-wrenching, less a sole tear or an escaping trickle from the eye and more an inconsolable aching. The music disappears, too. Physically present but mentally gone, haunted by an ongoing and incredibly traumatic event, the music seems to be preoccupied with this all-consuming grief, hardly able to process pain as the crushing weight of the strings continue to bear down upon the creaking stave. The residents are trapped in a horrific situation, and the melody can’t find a way to break out of its minor key, either. The single piano motif is important, as it seems to represent isolation, a singular sorrow, a loneliness and an inability to do anything about anything. Later, strings join the search party, weeping along with the piano. Life has to go on, but a sick mood hangs over the land. The soundtrack is heavy, but that only makes it all the more powerful. Soundtracks are often only reserved for film, although listeners have, in the past, been blessed with book-scores, like those in The Book Report series, so this somewhat novel (excuse me) approach is an area that can be further explored. Film will always offer strict representations and the forced digestion of its images, while the book is individual, creating its own imagery for every reader. The reader has to work in order to create the world. Likewise, music is subjective, too, but the book’s theme ensures sober music. The book’s meditation on loss requires a deep sensitivity, and Birkin ushers the strings to appropriate, and respectful, places, the piano gently bleeding from its emotional wounds. www.rjbirkin.bandcamp.com

Birkin为Jon McGregor同名小说创作的官方配乐，由英国中部的器乐三重奏Haiku Salut现场演奏并录制。评论将音乐与小说的核心主题——一个13岁少女Rebecca失踪后小镇居民承受的漫长创伤——紧密结合，弦乐在低音区缓慢膨胀，钢琴动机反复出现却始终被困在小调里，形成持续不断的悲恸感。评论特别提到Birkin的技术手段让作家在读书会现场将观众手机接入演出，使每次朗读都产生不同结果，这种交互式现场呈现方式为传统书籍配乐带来了新的维度。整体音乐沉重、内省，以克制的方式承载巨大的情感重量，评论认为小说中关于失落与时间的冥想气质在配乐中得到了忠实的延伸。

items.body: Olivier Alary’s compositions are draped over a misty scattering of naked trees. The season could be late autumn instead of early spring. Fiction / Non-Fiction is a collection of the composer’s film soundtrack work, which is imbued with a haunting atmosphere and a broad range of instrumentation. Accordion, saxophone, slide guitar, vibraphone, marimba, guitar, gongs, electronics, flute, double bass, clarinet and choir are all used, highlighting in marker pen a desire to give the music as full a life as possible. Remarkably, Fiction / Non-Fiction feels cohesive and surprisingly sparse when it could so easily have been cluttered. Slightly strange melodies slowly creep outside, moving from shadows into light, limping at a slanted angle which in turn gives the record a darkly unique sound. They sway as if in the middle of a tribal dance which to outsiders appears utterly alien. For the most part, the music is balletic and somewhat downtrodden, with a weak glow that is all but ready to fizzle out. Alary brings something fresh to an overpopulated genre, with the music becoming a bronze sunflower encircled by a growing number of weeds. A deep maturity rises like smoke from its slow vapours, echoing A Winged Victory for the Sullen or Stars of the Lid, lifting it up above the common. The composer has chosen to push the music beyond, embracing possibilities with an illimitable sound like that of evolution, carrying on its back a completely engaging and captivating style unlike anything else. A sliver of chrome light leaks out from the strings before trickling into the piano’s pool of flowing liquid. The pieces all flow as one, despite the album being labelled a collection. Its cool flavours give the album an original aftertaste. The smooth saxophone recedes into a fragile shell, becoming a paler, washed-out thing – as if it had just encountered a vampire – while its sultry colour leaks from every note, and the flute whispers over a tired breath of wind. The Montreal-based Frenchman, who has previously collaborated with Bjork, delivers a poetic album comprised of contemplative and deeply expressive composition. Rainy thoughts splash down onto the ground, and strings are soaked in grey hues. While the differing instruments naturally add colour to the album, it’s always pale and almost absent, tertiary and not primary. Fiction / Non-Fiction has a round form and gilded edges, but its inner space is dressed in an eternal shade of grey. www.130701.com

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑汇集了作曲家Olivier Alary为电影创作的原声音乐，涵盖手风琴、萨克斯、滑音吉他、颤音琴、马林巴琴、电子音效、长笛、低音提琴、单簧管及合唱等多种乐器，编织出层次丰富却不显拥挤的稀疏织体。旋律缓慢渗出，从阴影移向光亮，以倾斜的步伐展开，兼具芭蕾般的优雅与忧郁气质。评论将其与A Winged Victory for the Sullen、Stars of the Lid等当代氛围音乐标杆相提并论，强调其在成熟度与声音探索上的独特性。萨克斯音色时而温润时而褪色，长笛如疲惫的风声低语，弦乐浸泡在灰色调中，钢琴则像流动的液体池。整张专辑虽有圆融外形与金色边缘，内在却始终笼罩在永恒的灰色阴影下，呈现出统一而深沉的情绪氛围。

items.body: Long Story Short Dosed up on pretty high levels of reverb, Long Story Short is glistening, translucent music. Rain lightly falls as the bass note of an electric guitar sets the first stone in place. After that, soft sprinklings of notes are swept away on the perfumed, lilting air of major seventh chords. Appropriately titled ‘Lazing’, the music drifts by, seamlessly adding a little at a time. Like a cloud in the sky, it takes its time to fully form. Released on Too Many Fireworks, the ambient guitar music of Mateusz Franczak is sweet and soothing, at times lively and slightly frantic (which is unusual for the style of ambient guitar) without ever sounding cluttered, and at other times radiating a depthless serenity that ripples along with the reverb. The Polish experimental musician layers his ambient music with kindness, but there’s also a distorted, uneasy and thoroughly grey undercurrent in the depths of the ambient sound. That’s a mean feat in itself, because ambient music so often relies on its sparse vacuums that occupy the no-man’s-land between space and silence. The distorted intruder doesn’t dampen the slow, slightly melancholic feel, either. The notes ring and bleed together; the double stops clang with a muted tone that drags everything into a murky field of vision. A calming, casual tone captains the largely sedate music, its notes dimmed like the fine evening light of late spring. The shadows lurk just around the corner and are a couple of hours away from arriving, but as long as the music’s playing they never dare to creep out of their dark shells. A grittier sound sticks tightly to ‘Moving’. The prickly distortion is there, but it’s not strong enough to dampen the sound as a whole. The faces in the crowd appear to be crisper and sharper. Long Story Short takes a stride towards ambient song, too, the vocals gliding into a mini chorus that glows with the fiery heat of napalm. It gets its energy from both the soaring vocal and the spikier tone. Long Story Short lingers between structured song and improvised, sustaining soundscape, blearily straddling the ethereal and the everyday. Emerging out of this is a voice dripping with reverb, recalling the late Spacemen 3 and early Spritualized sound by way of a muddied, soulful drawl. The softer pools of a glorious, romanticized reverb evaporate in the light of a distorted tone that waddles out of the music’s swampy waters like a primeval crocodile. Paradise slips away and is replaced by the heady turbulence of uncertainty and doubt. The faith isn’t as strong as it was; the music’s glow is waning and swaying. Long Story Short is easily digestible, its colourful music as lulling as it is pressing. To a degree, Franczak’s history (he played in a number of rock and punk bands at an earlier age) influences the music’s lifeline, especially when it comes to the use of overdrive. It was, perhaps, inevitable, but it puts a different spin on the music. You get the feeling that Franczak really enjoyed the process. Long Story Short’s largely improvised, intoxicated melodies form a pleasant hybrid, where abrasive textures and passionate vocals blend in with ambient’s gentle curves. www.mateuszfranczak.bandcamp.com

items._cn_summary: 波兰实验音乐人Mateusz Franczak在独立厂牌Too Many Fireworks发表的吉他氛围专辑，以大量混响为基底，构建出透明而流动的声场。作品在漂浮的环境音色下埋藏失真与不安的暗流，合成器和声形成微妙的旋律碎片，慢速展开如云层成型。后期融入人声，借鉴Spacemen 3与早期Spiritualized的混响唱腔，在结构化歌曲与即兴音景之间游走。他早年摇滚与朋克经历对失真运用影响明显，使整体音色带有粗粝边缘，区别于传统ambient的留白美学，在甜美与阴郁、宁静与躁动之间持续切换张力。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家兼作曲家Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，延续斯洛伐克传统音乐与古典音乐的对话与融合。三个乐团参与演奏：Spectrum Quartett弦乐四重奏、传统风格四重奏Nogaband以及女声团体Ulijanky。曲目主要改编自斯洛伐克作曲家Eugen Suchoň的作品，并收录Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes以及曾深入斯洛伐克采风的匈牙利作曲家巴托克的创作。每首曲目的乐谱均注明了来自斯洛伐克乡村音乐的具体出处与演奏者，编排与演绎保留了传统声乐的能量与音色。评论强调这不是被管弦乐磨平棱角的版本，而是充满胆识、技巧与传统音乐灵魂的演奏，展现出演奏者与歌者对民间音乐的深入理解与沉浸。整体呈现一种古典语汇与民间根源相互回溯、相互滋养的紧密关系。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以乌克兰传统民歌为根基，聚焦俄罗斯占领区约两万乌克兰儿童被强制带往俄罗斯这一战争罪行主题。乌克兰裔加拿大歌手Marichka与bandurist歌手Alina Kuzma分别在加拿大和乌克兰召集两组全女性音乐家合作录制，编制以弓弦乐器为主，辅以班杜拉琴、钢琴与双陶笛等传统器乐。歌曲在传统与原创之间交织，如对传统歌谣《Foreign Land》的重新编排，将历史中少女被迫离家做工的叙事投射到当代被掳儿童的处境。音乐与声乐表现具备扎实的品质，演唱从温柔的抒情到激烈刚硬形成戏剧性对比。专辑在RootsWorld这样的世界音乐独立平台发行，具有明确的东欧文化视角与传统乐器融合特征。整体虽非实验或前卫范畴，但作为世界音乐领域的严肃创作，在主题深度与文化真实性上具有突出价值。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了圣多美和普林西比两个非洲小岛在1970至80年代录制的Puxa音乐，即所谓的非洲黄金时代之声。Puxa是一种复杂的节奏融合体，混合了其他前葡萄牙非洲殖民地的音乐元素，涵盖merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等多种风格，并被认为具有召唤或驱逐灵体的仪式功能。葡萄牙殖民者曾试图禁止Puxa舞蹈但显然未成功。这些岛屿尽管面积狭小、仅有12个村落，却孕育出层次丰富的吉他交织、应答式人声与绵长的律动骨架。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队展示了闷吉他短句与鼓组之间的角力，Sangazuza则展现了低音与键盘退场后鼓与吉他如何驱动舞者。Africa Negra的作品呈现了人声退让后音乐如何绵延铺展的典型场景，是了解非洲小众岛屿乐坛的珍贵档案。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa 厂牌推出的这张合辑聚焦贝宁传奇乐手 Antoine Dougbé 与 Orchestre Poly-Rythmo 合作期作品，跨度1977至1982年。Dougbé 以手拍大腿演绎名为 Cavacha 的节奏为核心创作模式，这种节拍源自鼓手 Belobi Meridjo 对火车节奏的提炼，后扩散至刚果流行乐。合辑在 Poly-Rythmo 此前以 Sato 和 Sakpata 巫毒传统为核心的基础上，加入了合成器音色与塑料质感吉他，明显呈现古巴 son 的影响，尤其是开篇曲目中人声呼叫应答与牛铃的运用。'Ma Won Min Towe Leo' 以合成器铺底展开，吉他在通鼓高帽节奏上交织，刚果伦巴元素贯穿其中。整体录制生涯虽短暂，但展现出西非流行乐在七十年代与加勒比及中部非洲音乐交汇时的丰富面貌。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio在专辑《Langs》中延续了对本土民间音乐的探索，但相较前作《Eventyrferd》中科幻合成器与传统素材的嫁接，本次回归更为'接地气'。主奏乐器高音萨克斯透露出爵士影响，开篇曲《Springleik》以挪威西部传统舞蹈旋律为基础，Egíl Kalman的低音提琴与Knut Kvifte Nesheim的鼓构成节奏骨架，再叠加Kalman的模块合成器与Nesheim的颤音琴丰富音色层次。三人的角色分配始终处于流动状态，Kalman在低音上接替旋律线与Hole齐奏，Nesheim则进一步拓展即兴空间，Hole在曲末再次奏出主题收束。整张专辑展现出爵士即兴、北欧民谣素材与电子声响之间的持续对话。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: 这张由瑞典小提琴手与两位挪威乐手合作的作品，以非传统方式重新诠释北欧传统舞曲素材。乐评指出三位音乐人各自有着跨越流派边界的经历——Mats Edén 深耕瑞典民间音乐并探索不同风格的融合，Tellef Kvifte 早在1970年代便参与挪威先锋跨界乐队 Slinkombas，常以竖笛、萨克斯、风笛等多样乐器演奏，其子 Knut Kvifte Nesheim 作为鼓手兼作曲家同样致力于模糊音乐类型界限。整张专辑虽以舞曲旋律为底，却更接近室内乐的气质：三位演奏者沉浸于亲密的音乐对话，而非为舞者伴奏的实用音乐。开篇选用的挪威塞特斯达尔小调 "Fossgrimen" 暗含神话意味——传说中瀑布精灵将提琴技艺传授给凡人，使其被视为魔鬼的乐器，乐评以此隐喻北欧舞曲表象之下的不安潜流。曲目的处理方式强调即兴碎片化与音色层次的探索，揭示了传统旋律中隐藏的可能性与暗面。
